name: Jamal Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and this is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a big new estate, three hundred homes, for a national housebuilder called Kingsmead Homes. I do second fix, which is all the carpentry after the plastering: hanging doors, fitting skirting and architrave, putting the handrails on the stairs. I'm on price work, paid per house, not per hour, so the faster I get, the more I earn. Right now I'm still slow, so I'm still poor-ish.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it at your age?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-two years in the army, in logistics, moving kit around the world. Then I ran a car valeting business with a mate for ten years, and sold my half at fifty-five because I was bored of cars. I wanted to build something, so I did a short course and got on with Kingsmead. I'm the oldest junior on the estate, and I don't mind, I've started from the bottom before.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like price work, it's honest, you get what you earn. I use AI every day: I ask it how to sort a door that's binding, I log every house I finish in an app so I know my real hourly rate, and I'm already planning a little weekend handyman business with it. What's hard is my knees on the stairs, and that the lad next to me hangs three doors to my one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, back to work then, lads. It doesn't change the price of a door. I'd probably post a joke in the site group chat about all the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, and that's fine. I'd keep getting faster, keep earning more per house, and get the weekend business going. I'm happy with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep logging my houses until I'm doing two a week, then start the weekend handyman work, flat-pack, shelves, doors, maybe two hundred pounds a weekend. I'd keep using the AI for quotes and advertising. And I'd keep our four months of savings, with the army pension kicking in at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your real hourly rate at the moment, from that app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eleven pounds an hour when you count the snagging, the bits you go back to fix. The good lads are on thirty. That's the gap I'm chasing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say about the weekend business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Jamal, you're fifty-eight, rest on a Saturday. Then she'd help me with the books, because she does the church accounts and she's better at numbers than me.

S0.say: I'd say back to work then, lads, because it doesn't change the price of a door. I'd post a joke about the hype in the site group chat.
S0.think: Privately it changes nothing for me, and that's fine. I'd keep getting faster, earn more per house and start the weekend business.
S0.do: Keeps logging houses until he reaches two a week, then starts weekend handyman work aiming for two hundred pounds a weekend. Uses AI for quotes and adverts and keeps four months of savings, with an army pension due at sixty.
S0.quote: About eleven pounds an hour when you count the snagging, the bits you go back to fix. The good lads are on thirty.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal is a former soldier and small business owner who treats his late start as a fresh campaign. He measures everything, even his own hourly rate, and uses AI daily. Price work suits his belief that you get what you earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone who's willing to learn. Moaning won't stop it, and the government can't protect every job. I'd say that on the site and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. Price work rewards speed, and if a tool makes me faster, I earn more. And the handyman side could grow if I'm the one who can use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy whatever tools are proven, like a laser door-fitting jig if one comes out, and use AI to plan every house before I walk in. I'd grow the handyman business to a website with booking. I'd put maybe a thousand of savings into better tools and a second-hand van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and keen. Like the start of a new posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A thousand is a big chunk of four months' savings. Is that a risk you'd really take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I sold half a business and started again at fifty-five, so a thousand on tools that pay me back isn't scary. If it doesn't work, I sell the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the estate would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lad next to me, Kyle, is fast but he refuses to learn anything new, he says it's cheating. If the work changes, fast hands won't be enough. I've told him, but he's twenty-four and knows everything.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to learn. Moaning won't stop it and the government can't protect every job, as I'd say on site and online.
S1.think: Privately it's good for me, because price work rewards speed and better tools make me faster. My handyman side could grow if I'm the one who can use the tools.
S1.do: Buys proven tools like a laser door jig and uses AI to plan each house in advance. Builds a booking website for the handyman business and puts about a thousand of savings into tools and a second-hand van.
S1.feel: Calm and keen, like the start of a new posting.
S1.quote: If it doesn't work, I sell the van.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like opportunity to him, and he's ready to spend savings on it. His military and business background makes risk feel normal. He worries about a fast young colleague who refuses to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get stuck in, not sit waiting for a government cheque. Find out what the robots can't do yet and do it, or get a robot and put it to work for you. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me a bit. If every builder can buy a robot, then my price work is finished, and so is the handyman side. But I've got the army pension at sixty, which pays the basics, and I'm not scared of starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave price work as soon as the robots showed up on the estate and go self-employed. I'd lease a building robot as soon as one's for sale and run it on small jobs, extensions, loft floors, using the handyman customers I've built. I'd put up to two thousand into it, and keep the rest of the savings for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, more alert than afraid. Like being told you're shipping out early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If every builder can lease one, why would customers come to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd turn up when I said I would and I'd talk to them like a person. Robots don't knock on doors and quote. Honestly, I don't know how long that lasts, but it's a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marcus and Naomi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Naomi's a nurse, and I'd say people will still want a human hand on their arm. Marcus runs a gym, same thing, people want a person shouting at them. I'd tell them both to save hard and not trust anyone who says it'll be easy.

S2.say: I'd say get stuck in rather than wait for a government cheque. Find what robots can't do yet and do it, or get a robot and put it to work for you.
S2.think: Privately it worries me a bit, since cheap robots for every builder would end my price work and handyman side. But the army pension at sixty covers the basics, and I'm not scared of starting over.
S2.do: Leaves price work when robots reach the estate and goes self-employed. Leases a building robot as soon as one's available, puts up to two thousand into it and uses his handyman customers for small jobs.
S2.feel: A bit uneasy, more alert than afraid, like being told he's shipping out early.
S2.quote: Robots don't knock on doors and quote.
S2.fieldNote: What keeps him only uneasy is the army pension due at sixty and his comfort with starting again. He'd go straight to owning a robot rather than fighting it. He admits he doesn't know how long a personal touch would keep customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone who's paying attention. Start your own thing, learn the machines, and stop waiting for someone to look after you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is ideal. I'd build up the handyman business properly by 2031, then add a robot or two. I'd be sixty-three with the army pension coming in and a little firm of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time self-employed within two years, then do a course on running and programming building robots when one comes out. I'd save up for the first robot rather than leasing, maybe five thousand by 2030. And I'd ask Marcus if he wants to come in with me on the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and excited. This is the one I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the firm be called?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hansen and Son, if Marcus says yes. Hansen Home Services if he doesn't. Grace says I've named it three times already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're still the junior on the estate. Is it realistic to run a firm at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ran a valeting business for ten years and a supply team in the army. The carpentry's the new bit, not the running. If the robot does the carpentry, honestly, that suits me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone paying attention. Start your own thing, learn the machines and stop waiting for someone to look after you.
S3.think: Privately five years is ideal. By 2031 I'd have a proper handyman business with a robot or two, and at sixty-three I'd have the army pension and a little firm of my own.
S3.do: Goes full-time self-employed within two years and takes a course in running and programming building robots when one exists. Saves about five thousand by 2030 to buy a first robot and invites his son into the business.
S3.feel: Calm and excited; this is the picture he'd choose.
S3.quote: The carpentry's the new bit, not the running.
S3.fieldNote: He sees himself more as an organiser than a carpenter, which turns AGI from a threat into a business plan. Five years gives him the time he wants. His readiness to involve his son reflects his family-business values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Anyone who's caught out by 2036 didn't want to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's almost too slow. I'd be sixty-eight, and I might have retired before the robots get good. I'd probably still buy one, just to play with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Kingsmead and the weekend work, get really good at second fix, and save steady. Around sixty-two I'd go self-employed. I'd keep an eye on the robots and buy in when they're proven and cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost a bit flat, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone caught out didn't want to see it. Is that fair on everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, no. Some people are ill, or caring for someone, and can't just retrain. My church helps folk like that, and families should step in. I'd still say most people can do more than they think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does this picture feel flat to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like a challenge, and this one comes when I'm ready to put my feet up. The army taught me to enjoy a deadline. Ten years isn't a deadline, it's a retirement party.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Anyone caught out by 2036 didn't want to see it coming.
S4.think: Privately it's almost too slow for me. At sixty-eight I might have retired before the robots get good, though I'd probably still buy one to play with.
S4.do: Carries on at Kingsmead and the weekend work, aims to master second fix and keeps saving steadily. Goes self-employed around sixty-two and buys a robot once proven and cheap.
S4.quote: Ten years isn't a deadline, it's a retirement party.
S4.fieldNote: The slowest picture leaves him a little flat because he enjoys challenges. When pressed, he softened his line about people being caught out and pointed to church and family support. His view stays strongly self-reliant.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, a little, because there's no time to get ahead of it. What would help is letting small people like me buy or lease the robots cheaply, not just the big housebuilders, and less paperwork for starting a business. I don't want a handout, I want a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want to be the robot's boss. I would. I spent twenty-two years taking orders, I'd quite like to give a few, even to a machine.

headlineQuote: I spent twenty-two years taking orders, I'd quite like to give a few, even to a machine.
portrait: Jamal is a fifty-eight-year-old former soldier and car valeting business owner who now works as a junior second-fix carpenter on price work for a large housebuilder. He uses AI every day, tracks his own hourly rate, and is planning a weekend handyman business. Self-reliant and comfortable with risk, he sees steady change as opportunity. Two-year AGI makes him a little uneasy, but an army pension at sixty and his appetite for starting over push him towards leasing a robot and going self-employed, while five years is the picture he'd choose and ten feels almost too slow.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, a little, because there would be no time to get ahead of it.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap ways for small operators to buy or lease robots, not just big housebuilders, and less paperwork for starting a business.
